scenes.text: The poet drives to Cochin airport with her mother beside her.
The mother dozes, her face pale 'as a late winter's moon'.
At security, the poet hides her fear: 'see you soon, Amma', and smiles.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Kamala Das** (1934–2009). It captures the fear of losing an ageing parent and the effort to hide that pain.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Driving from her parents' home to Cochin airport, the poet sees her mother dozing, mouth open, her face 'ashen like that of a corpse'. She realises with pain that her mother is old and close to death.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: She looks away at the young trees 'sprinting' and children 'spilling out of their homes' — images of youth and energy contrasting with her mother's age.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: At the airport security check she looks again at her mother, 'wan, pale as a late winter's moon'. Her childhood fear returns, but she says only 'see you soon, Amma', and smiles, smiles, smiles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paraphrasing lines without explaining their meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the words.
- Forgetting the poet's name and central idea in the opening line.

scenes.text: The poet asks the whole world to count to twelve and keep still.
No fishermen harming whales, no wars, no hurry.
Like the earth in winter, silence brings new life.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by Chilean poet **Pablo Neruda** (Nobel 1971). It calls for a moment of silence and introspection to end violence and self-destruction.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: The poet asks us to count up to twelve and keep still, without speaking any language, without moving our arms so much. It would be an 'exotic moment' without rush or engines; all would be together in sudden strangeness.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Fishermen would not harm whales; the man gathering salt would look at his hurt hands. Those preparing green wars, wars with gas, wars with fire, victories with no survivors, would put on clean clothes and walk with their brothers.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He clarifies he does not want 'total inactivity' — 'life is what it is about; I want no truck with death'. If we were not so single-minded about keeping our lives moving, a huge silence might interrupt the sadness of never understanding ourselves. 'Perhaps the Earth can teach us / as when everything seems dead / and later proves to be alive.' Now he'll count to twelve, and we'll keep quiet, and he will go.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paraphrasing lines without explaining their meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the words.
- Forgetting the poet's name and central idea in the opening line.

scenes.text: A daffodil, a shady bower, a clear stream.
Life has gloom, despondence and 'unhealthy and o'er-darkened ways'.
Beauty lifts 'the pall from our dark spirits'.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: An extract from *Endymion* by **John Keats** (1795–1821), English Romantic poet. It opens with the famous line 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever'.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: A thing of beauty is a joy for ever; its loveliness increases and never passes into nothingness. It keeps a quiet bower for us and a sleep full of sweet dreams, health and quiet breathing.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Every morning we weave a 'flowery band' to bind us to the earth, despite despondence, the lack of noble natures, gloomy days and unhealthy ways. Some shape of beauty removes the pall (gloom) from our dark spirits.

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Such things are the sun, the moon, trees old and young, daffodils with the green world they live in, clear rills (streams), the mid-forest brake with musk-rose blooms, and the grandeur of the 'mighty dead' and lovely tales. They are 'an endless fountain of immortal drink, / Pouring unto us from the heaven's brink.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paraphrasing lines without explaining their meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the words.
- Forgetting the poet's name and central idea in the opening line.

scenes.text: Farmers set up a little roadside stand to sell berries and squash.
City cars rush past without a glance.
The poet feels the pain of rural poverty.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Robert Frost** (1874–1963), American poet, about the neglect of rural poor by city dwellers and the false promises of 'greedy good-doers'.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: An old house puts out a new shed in front at the edge of the road, selling wild berries and squash. The farmers want a share of city money to 'flower' their lives. Cars pass by, never noticing; if one stops, it's to ask the way or turn, or someone complains the signs spoil the landscape.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: The poet mentions the plan to move country people into villages near theatres and stores, where 'greedy good-doers' and 'beneficent beasts of prey' will 'take care' of them — so they will 'sleep' (lose independence).

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He feels the 'childish longing in vain' at the window, waiting for a car to stop. He imagines putting them out of their pain at once, but then thinks how he would feel if someone did that to him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paraphrasing lines without explaining their meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the words.
- Forgetting the poet's name and central idea in the opening line.

scenes.text: Aunt Jennifer embroiders bright, fearless tigers.
Her husband's wedding ring sits heavily on her hand.
She will die, but the tigers will go on prancing.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A poem by **Adrienne Rich** (1929–2012), American feminist poet. It contrasts a woman oppressed in marriage with the free, confident tigers she creates in her art.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Aunt Jennifer's tigers prance across a screen — 'bright topaz denizens of a world of green'. They do not fear the men beneath the tree; they pace in 'sleek chivalric certainty'.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Her fingers flutter through the wool; she finds even the ivory needle hard to pull. 'The massive weight of Uncle's wedding band / Sits heavily upon Aunt Jennifer's hand.'

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: When she is dead, her terrified hands will lie still, ringed with the ordeals she was mastered by. But the tigers she made will go on prancing, proud and unafraid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paraphrasing lines without explaining their meaning.
- Naming a device without quoting the words.
- Forgetting the poet's name and central idea in the opening line.

scenes.text: Charley, 31, says he found a third level at Grand Central Station, New York.

steps.title: About the text
steps.body: A story by **Jack Finney** blending reality and fantasy. It explores escapism from the stress of modern life and the borderline between time and the mind.

steps.title: Summary — part 1
steps.body: Charley tells us the New York Central and New York, New Haven and Hartford railroads say there are only two levels at Grand Central — but he has been on the third level. His psychiatrist friend Sam says it is a 'waking-dream wish fulfilment' to escape modern insecurity, fear and war.

steps.title: Summary — part 2
steps.body: Taking a short cut one night, Charley found himself in an older station with brass spittoons, gas lights and passengers in 1890s clothes; a newspaper dated 11 June 1894. steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: He changed $300 into old-style currency, but never found the third level again. Sam disappeared. Charley later found among his grandfather's stamp collection a first-day cover letter postmarked 18 July 1894, from Sam in Galesburg, saying he'd found the third level and urging them to keep looking.

steps.title: About the text

steps.title: Summary — part 3

steps.title: About the text

steps.title: Summary — part 1

She learned that shingled (cut) hair was for cowards among her people. She hid under a bed but was dragged out and her long hair was cut. She felt she had lost her spirit, like 'one of many little animals driven by a herder'.

steps.title: Summary — part 2

steps.title: Summary — part 3
steps.body: Bama studied hard, stood first in her class, and many people became her friends. Both writers protest discrimination — racial and caste-based — and show the dignity of resistance.

steps.title: IP
steps.body:
- **Patent:** protects a new, inventive, industrially useful invention; granted for **20 years** from filing in India (Patents Act 1970).
- **Trademark:** protects name, logo, slogan identifying goods or services; registration valid 10 years and renewable (Trade Marks Act 1999).
- **Copyright:** protects original literary, artistic, musical and software works; generally the author's life plus 60 years for many works (Copyright Act 1957).
- **Design registration** protects appearance (15 years in total in India); **Geographical Indication** (e.g. Darjeeling tea).
Ideas alone are not protected; their expression/application is.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A brand's logo → trademark. A new water filter mechanism → patent. A song or book → copyright. Basmati-like regional product name → GI.

scenes.text: A tea stall sells a cup for ₹15; each cup costs ₹9 in ingredients, cup and gas.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Gross profit** = sales − cost of goods sold. **Gross margin %** = gross profit ÷ sales × 100.
- **Net profit** = gross profit − operating expenses (rent, wages, electricity). **Net margin %** = net profit ÷ sales × 100.
- **Markup %** = profit ÷ cost × 100.
- Unit contribution = price − variable cost per unit.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Sales 300 cups × ₹15 = ₹4,500; COGS 300 × ₹9 = ₹2,700 → gross profit ₹1,800 → gross margin 1,800 ÷ 4,500 = **40%**. Rent + wages ₹1,200 → net profit ₹600 → net margin 600 ÷ 4,500 = **13.3%**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing gross and net profit, or using cost instead of sales as the margin denominator.

scenes.text: A garment supplier delivers goods on 60 days' credit but must pay for cloth in 15 days.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Working capital** = current assets − current liabilities; it funds day-to-day operations. **Cash flow** = cash in − cash out; a profitable firm can still run short of cash if customers pay late. **Operating cycle** = days to convert cash → stock → sales → cash. **Receivable days** = (receivables ÷ sales) × days.
Help: shorter credit, advance payments, negotiating supplier terms, inventory control.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Current assets ₹3,00,000; current liabilities ₹1,80,000 → working capital **₹1,20,000**. Monthly sales ₹2,40,000 with receivables ₹1,20,000 → receivable days = 1,20,000 ÷ 2,40,000 × 30 = **15 days**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Treating profit as cash in the bank.

steps.title: Forms
steps.body:
- **Sole proprietorship:** one owner, simple, unlimited liability.
- **Partnership:** 2+ partners with a deed; unlimited liability (Partnership Act 1932).
- **LLP:** partners' liability limited (LLP Act 2008).
- **Private limited company:** separate legal entity, limited liability, compliance heavier (Companies Act 2013).
- Also: **Udyam registration** for MSMEs, GST registration where thresholds apply, shop/establishment licence, FSSAI for food, trade licence.
Choose by liability, funding needs, tax and compliance. Take professional advice.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Planning to raise investor money and issue shares → private limited company. A solo freelance tutor with small income → sole proprietorship.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking a sole proprietor has limited liability; it is unlimited. General education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Plan

school-c12-geography.title: Class 12 Geography · Fundamentals of Human Geography
school-c12-geography.description: Chapter courses for Class 12 human geography: nature and scope, world population, human development and primary activities — with case studies, maps described in words, numericals and source/case-based practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Human Geography: Nature and Scope
courses.summary: What human geography is, the interaction of nature and humans (environmental determinism, possibilism, neo-determinism), the history of approaches and the fields and sub-fields of human geography.
outcomes: Learners can define human geography with standard definitions
Learners can compare determinism, possibilism and neo-determinism with examples
Learners can trace broad stages in the development of human geography
Learners can relate sub-fields to sister disciplines
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Benda, of the Abujh Maad area in central India, collects herbs, fruit and honey from the forest and knows every path.
Far away in a big city, a software engineer's life is shaped far more by technology than by forests.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Human geography studies the **interrelationship between the physical environment and the socio-cultural environment** created by humans. Classical definitions:
- **Ratzel**: synthetic study of relationships between human societies and the earth's surface.
- **Ellen C. Semple**: study of the changing relationship between unresting humans and the unstable earth.
- **Paul Vidal de la Blache**: a conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing the earth and the relations between living beings inhabiting it.

steps.title: Naturalisation of humans → humanisation of nature
steps.body:
- **Environmental determinism**: in early stages, with little technology, nature dictated life — people adapted, feared and worshipped nature (Benda's story).
- **Possibilism**: with technology, humans create possibilities; nature offers opportunities, humans choose — imprints of human activity everywhere (fields, cities, ports).
- **Neo-determinism** (**Griffith Taylor**): **'stop and go' determinism** — like traffic lights; humans can develop but must respect nature's limits. No situation is absolute necessity or absolute freedom.

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body: Desert farmers using canals and drip irrigation (Indira Gandhi Canal) = **possibilism**. Choosing not to build on steep fragile Himalayan slopes to avoid landslides = **neo-determinism**. Hunter-gatherers moving with seasons = **determinism**.

steps.title: Solved: why 'stop and go'?
steps.body: Climate change, pollution and resource depletion show unchecked possibilism harms the environment. Neo-determinism argues for sustainable development — go ahead where nature allows, stop when limits are crossed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Neo-determinism is by **Griffith Taylor**, not Ratzel.

activity.prompt: Determinism, possibilism or neo-determinism?

items.text: Benda's life fully dependent on the forest
Greenhouses growing vegetables in snowy regions
Limiting construction in a flood plain
Worshipping rivers and fearing storms in early societies
Building ports and cities on reclaimed land
Development within ecological limits ('stop and go')

quiz.q: 'Stop and go determinism' was proposed by:
'Unresting man and unstable earth' is from:

scenes.text: Early explorers wrote travel accounts of distant lands.
Today geographers analyse satellite images and census data with GIS.

steps.title: Broad stages
steps.body:
- **Colonial period**: exploration and description; imperial and trade interests.
- **Later colonial**: regional analysis — regions studied in detail as part of the whole.
- **Interwar (1930s)**: **areal differentiation** — why regions differ.
- **Late 1950s–1960s**: **spatial organisation** — quantitative revolution, computers and statistics.
- **1970s**: **humanistic, radical and behavioural** schools — dissatisfaction with quantitative approach; focus on human awareness, poverty, inequality (radical — Marxian), behaviour.
- **1990s**: **post-modernism** — grand generalisations questioned; local context emphasised.

steps.title: Fields and sister disciplines
steps.body:
- Social geography → sociology (behavioural, perception, social welfare, leisure, cultural, gender, historical, medical geography).
- **Urban geography** → urban studies & planning.
- **Political geography** → political science (electoral, military).
- **Population geography** → demography.
- **Settlement geography** → urban/rural planning.
- **Economic geography** → economics (resource, agricultural, industrial, marketing, tourism, international trade).

steps.title: Solved: why did humanistic geography arise?
steps.body: 1) Quantitative models ignored human feelings and values. 2) Geographers wanted to study awareness, agency and perception. 3) So humanistic geography focused on the role of human agency.

steps.title: Solved: matching
steps.body: Medical geography links with epidemiology; electoral geography with psephology; gender geography with women's studies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The quantitative revolution came in the late 1950s–60s, before the humanistic/radical schools of the 1970s.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Case-based questions: identify concept → justify with lines from the case → give a real example.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
courses.summary: Where people live and why, density, components and trends of population growth, migration push and pull factors, demographic transition and population control.
outcomes: Learners can explain uneven distribution with geographical, economic and social factors
Learners can calculate density, growth rate and doubling time
Learners can explain the demographic transition theory with stages
Learners can classify migration push and pull factors
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: In the Ganga plains, villages sit just a few km apart.
In the Sahara you can drive for hours without seeing a house.

steps.title: Uneven distribution
steps.body: About **90%** of the world's people live on about **10%** of its land. The 10 most populous countries hold about **60%** of world population. Dense areas: **East Asia, South Asia, Western Europe, north-eastern USA**. Sparse: high latitudes, deserts, rainforests, high mountains. World population crossed **8 billion** in **November 2022** (UN estimate).

steps.title: Factors
steps.body: **Geographical**: water availability, landforms (flat plains), climate (moderate), soils (fertile). **Economic**: minerals (Katanga–Zambia copper belt), urbanisation (jobs, services), industrialisation (Kobe–Osaka). **Social and cultural**: religious or cultural significance (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican), political unrest/war drives people away.

steps.title: Density
steps.body: **Density = Population ÷ Area** (persons per km²). Example: 1,000,000 people on 4,000 km² → 250 per km².

steps.title: Solved: density
steps.body: A state has 72 million people and 308,000 km². Density = 72,000,000 / 308,000 ≈ **234 persons/km²**.

steps.title: Solved: explain a pattern
steps.body: Why is the Nile valley densely populated within a desert? 1) Water from the Nile. 2) Fertile alluvial soil. 3) Long history of irrigated agriculture — geography concentrated people in a narrow strip.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Density uses area, not number of households. Units: persons per km².

activity.prompt: A district has 2,450,000 people and an area of 3,500 km². What is its population density (persons per km²)?

scenes.text: The world took all of history until around 1800 to reach 1 billion people.
It added the most recent billion in about 11 years.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Births**: Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = live births per 1,000 population per year.
- **Deaths**: Crude Death Rate (CDR) = deaths per 1,000 per year.
- **Migration**: immigration (in), emigration (out).
**Natural growth** = births − deaths. **Actual growth** = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. Growth can be **positive** or **negative**.

steps.title: Trends
steps.body: Growth was slow for most of history. Since the 18th–19th centuries — agricultural improvements, industrial revolution, medicine, sanitation — death rates fell and growth accelerated. Doubling time shortened drastically. Many developed countries now have low or negative growth; much of the growth today is in parts of Asia and Africa.

steps.title: Solved: natural growth rate
steps.body: CBR 20, CDR 7 → natural increase = 13 per 1,000 = **1.3%** per year.

steps.title: Solved: doubling time (rule of 70)
steps.body: Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (%). At 1.4% → 70/1.4 = **50 years**. At 3.5% → 20 years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: CBR is per 1,000 — convert to % by dividing by 10.

activity.prompt: A country has CBR 24 and CDR 10 per 1,000 with no migration. Using the rule of 70, about how many years will it take to double?

scenes.text: Ramesh leaves his flood-prone village for a textile job in Surat.
Meanwhile, his parents' generation had seven children; he plans two.

steps.title: Push and pull
steps.body:
**Push** (origin less attractive): unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics, socio-economic backwardness.
**Pull** (destination attractive): better jobs, living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, pleasant climate.

steps.title: Demographic transition theory
steps.body:
Explains change from **high births & high deaths** to **low births & low deaths** as societies move from rural-agrarian-illiterate to urban-industrial-literate.
- **Stage 1**: high fertility and mortality; slow growth; low life expectancy; mostly agriculture.
- **Stage 2**: fertility stays high early then declines; mortality falls fast (health, sanitation) → **population explosion**.
- **Stage 3**: both low; population stable or slowly growing; urban, literate, high technical know-how, deliberate control of family size.

steps.title: Population control
steps.body: Family planning, access to contraception, education of girls, health care, incentives; **Thomas Malthus (1798)** argued population grows faster than food supply — checks would come through famine, disease, war.

steps.title: Solved: identify stage
steps.body: CBR 35, CDR 10 → wide gap, rapid growth → **Stage 2**. CBR 10, CDR 9 → **Stage 3**.

steps.title: Solved: classify factors
steps.body: Floods in village → push. Factory jobs in Surat → pull. Better schools in city → pull.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In Stage 2 it is **deaths** that fall first, not births.

activity.prompt: Push or pull?

scenes.text: A city planning office gives you census figures.
Recommend schools and hospitals for the next decade.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: City: population 2.0 million; CBR 18; CDR 6; net in-migration 10 per 1,000. Actual growth = 18 − 6 + 10 = 22 per 1,000 = 2.2% per year.

steps.title: Tip
steps.body: Rule of 70: 70/2.2 ≈ 32 years to double.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting migration when computing actual growth.

activity.prompt: Using actual growth of 2.2% per year (simple, not compound), how many people will a city of 2,000,000 add in one year?

options: Low fertility from urbanisation, education, women's employment

options: Both true; R doesn't explain A

courses.title: Ch 3 · Human Development
courses.summary: Growth versus development, the concept of human development (Mahbub ul Haq, Amartya Sen), its four pillars, approaches, and how the Human Development Index is measured and interpreted.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish growth from development
Learners can explain the four pillars of human development
Learners can compare income, welfare, basic needs and capability approaches
Learners can interpret HDI dimensions and categories
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Growth, development and the four pillars

scenes.text: Town X's GDP doubles, but children still drop out of school and hospitals are far away.
Town Y grows slowly but invests in schools and clinics — people live longer, freer lives.

steps.title: Growth vs development
steps.body: **Growth** is **quantitative** and value-neutral — an increase (can be positive or negative). **Development** is **qualitative** and always positive — a qualitative change. Growth does not automatically mean development.

steps.title: Human development
steps.body: The idea was introduced by Pakistani economist **Dr Mahbub ul Haq**, who created the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, first published by **UNDP in 1990**. He described human development as development that **enlarges people's choices** and improves their lives. **Prof. Amartya Sen** saw development as increasing **freedom** (removing 'unfreedoms'); his **capability** approach underlies HDI. Key capabilities: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and access to resources for a decent life.

steps.title: Four pillars
steps.body:
- **Equity**: equal access to opportunities regardless of gender, race, income, caste.
- **Sustainability**: continuity of opportunities for future generations.
- **Productivity**: human labour productivity — enriched by building people's capabilities.
- **Empowerment**: having the power to make choices — through good governance and people-oriented policies.

steps.title: Solved: apply the pillars
steps.body: A scheme gives free bicycles to girls to reach secondary school. **Equity** (gender access), **empowerment** (choice to study), **productivity** (future skills).

steps.title: Solved: growth without development
steps.body: Town X: GDP up but schooling and health poor → growth without development. Town Y shows that choices widened even with slower growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: HDI was created by Mahbub ul Haq (with Sen's ideas), not by the World Bank.

activity.prompt: Match the pillar to the example
pairs: Equal school admission for Dalit and tribal children
Women's self-help groups making their own loan decisions

quiz.q: HDI was first published by UNDP in:

scenes.text: Each year UNDP publishes a 'report card' ranking countries on human development.
Some oil-rich countries rank lower than their income suggests.

steps.title: Four approaches
steps.body:
- **Income approach**: oldest; human development linked to income.
- **Welfare approach**: humans as beneficiaries of development; government spends on education, health, social security.
- **Basic needs approach**: initially proposed by the **ILO**; six basic needs — health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, housing; human choices ignored.
- **Capability approach**: **Amartya Sen** — building capabilities in health, education and access to resources is the key.

steps.title: HDI dimensions
steps.body:
Score between **0 and 1**.
- **Health**: life expectancy at birth.
- **Education**: (adult literacy and gross enrolment in older reports;) now **mean years of schooling** and **expected years of schooling**.
- **Access to resources**: purchasing power — **GNI per capita (PPP, US$)**.
Each dimension originally had equal weight (1/3). **Human Poverty Index** measured shortfall; **Gross National Happiness** (Bhutan) is an alternative measure.

steps.title: Categories
steps.body: UNDP groups countries: **very high** (0.800 and above), **high** (0.700–0.799), **medium** (0.550–0.699), **low** (below 0.550).

steps.title: Solved: simple average
steps.body: If a country's health index = 0.80, education = 0.60, income = 0.70, a simple arithmetic average = (0.80 + 0.60 + 0.70)/3 = **0.70** → 'high'. (UNDP now uses a geometric mean; result ≈ 0.695, borderline medium — showing how method matters.)

steps.title: Solved: why rich ≠ high HDI
steps.body: Income may be concentrated; spending on health and education may be low; gender inequality may limit opportunities. So HDI rank can be below income rank.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: HDI is not GDP. And HDI does not include happiness — Bhutan's GNH does.

activity.prompt: Health index 0.90, education index 0.75, income index 0.84. What is the simple arithmetic average (2 decimals)?

quiz.q: Basic needs approach was proposed by:
Access to resources is measured by:
Gross National Happiness is associated with:

scenes.text: A district has low schooling, decent income, and poor maternal health.
You have one budget — where does it raise human development most?

steps.title: Think
steps.body: Which HDI dimension is weakest? Which pillar would your policy serve?

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: In long answers, define human development, give pillars with examples, and explain HDI with dimensions and categories.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming more factories automatically raise HDI.

choices.label: Schools, teachers and girls' enrolment drives
choices.feedback: Education is the weakest dimension — largest gain.

choices.label: Subsidise a new mall

choices.feedback: Health is a core HDI dimension.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Primary Activities
courses.summary: Gathering, hunting, pastoralism (nomadic herding and commercial ranching), the types of agriculture from shifting cultivation to plantations, dairy, Mediterranean and cooperative/collective farming, and mining.
outcomes: Learners can classify primary activities with world regions
Learners can compare nomadic herding and commercial livestock rearing
Learners can describe each type of agriculture with locations
Learners can explain factors and methods of mining
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A Gaddi shepherd of Himachal climbs to high meadows in summer.
As snow arrives, he brings his flock down to the plains.

steps.title: Gathering and hunting
steps.body: Oldest activities. Gathering is practised in harsh climates: high latitudes (**northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile**), and low latitudes (**Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern Australia, interior south-east Asia**). Modern gathering is market-oriented: quinine, tannin, latex, medicines, chicle (chewing gum) — but synthetic substitutes reduce demand.

steps.title: Nomadic herding
steps.body: Herders move with animals for water and pasture. Regions: (1) **Atlantic coast of North Africa → Arabian peninsula → Mongolia and Central China**; (2) **Tundra** of Eurasia (reindeer); (3) **south-west Africa and Madagascar**. Animals: cattle (tropical Africa), sheep, goats, camels (Sahara, Asian deserts), yak and llamas (Tibet, Andes), reindeer (Arctic). **Transhumance**: seasonal migration between plains and mountains — in India: **Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis, Bhotiyas**.

steps.title: Commercial livestock rearing
steps.body: **Ranching** — large permanent ranches divided into parcels fenced to regulate grazing; specialised in one animal; scientific breeding, disease control, processing for export. Regions: **New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay, USA**.

steps.title: Solved: compare
steps.body: Nomadic: subsistence, moving, mixed herds, traditional methods. Commercial: market, fixed ranches, one animal type, scientific methods, capital-intensive.

steps.title: Solved: why is nomadic herding declining?
steps.body: 1) Political boundaries restrict movement. 2) Governments settle nomads. 3) New settlements and farming reduce pasture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Transhumance is **seasonal** movement between regions; it is not random wandering.

activity.prompt: Match the animal to its nomadic region

scenes.text: A family clears and burns a forest patch on a hillside and plants rice and vegetables.
After a few years the soil tires, and they move to a new patch.

steps.title: Primitive subsistence (shifting cultivation)
steps.body: Slash and burn; tools are simple; ash adds fertility; cultivated for a few years then abandoned. Names: **jhum** (north-eastern India), **milpa** (Central America & Mexico), **ladang** (Indonesia & Malaysia). The jhum cycle has shortened, reducing fertility recovery.

steps.title: Intensive subsistence
steps.body: Densely populated **monsoon Asia**. (a) **Paddy-dominated** — small holdings, family labour, intensive use of land, manure; (b) **non-paddy** — wheat, soybean, barley, sorghum (north China, Manchuria, North Korea, North Japan) with irrigation.

steps.title: Plantation agriculture
steps.body: Introduced by Europeans in their colonies: large estates, heavy capital, scientific methods, cheap labour, single-crop specialisation, good transport to factories and ports. Examples: **tea and coffee in India and Sri Lanka**, **rubber in Malaysia**, **sugarcane and bananas in West Indies**, **cocoa and coffee in West Africa**, **coffee in Brazil (fazendas)**. Many are now owned by governments or nationals.

steps.title: Solved: why is shifting cultivation unsustainable now?
steps.body: Population growth shortened the fallow period; forests have no time to regenerate; soil loses fertility; erosion on slopes increases.

steps.title: Solved: features of plantations
steps.body: 1) Large estates. 2) Capital-intensive. 3) Managerial and technical support. 4) Monoculture. 5) Transport network linking estates to processing and markets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Milpa is Central America/Mexico; ladang is Indonesia/Malaysia — don't swap.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its region

quiz.q: Intensive paddy farming is typical of:

scenes.text: On the Canadian Prairies, one family harvests hundreds of hectares with combines.
In Jharkhand, a coal mine works an open-cast pit.

steps.title: Extensive commercial grain
steps.body: Interior semi-arid mid-latitude grasslands: **Prairies** (N. America), **Steppes** (Eurasia), **Pampas** (Argentina), **Velds** (South Africa), **Downs** (Australia), **Canterbury plains** (New Zealand). Huge farms (hundreds of hectares), highly mechanised, low yield per acre but high yield per person; main crop wheat.

steps.title: Mixed, dairy, Mediterranean, market gardening
steps.body:
- **Mixed farming**: crops + livestock; NW Europe, eastern N. America, parts of Eurasia, southern continents; high capital on machinery and buildings; crop rotation, intercropping.
- **Dairy farming**: most advanced and efficient type of rearing; capital and labour intensive; near urban markets; NW Europe, Canada, SE Australia, NZ, Tasmania.
- **Mediterranean**: both sides of Mediterranean Sea, central California, central Chile, SW South Africa, SW Australia; citrus, **viticulture** (grapes for wine).
- **Market gardening & horticulture**: high-value crops near cities; **truck farming** — distance a truck covers overnight.

steps.title: Cooperative and collective
steps.body: **Cooperative**: farmers pool resources — successful in **Denmark, Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Italy**. **Collective** (kolkhoz): introduced in the former **USSR** — means of production owned socially; farmers got a share; could keep a small plot.

steps.title: Mining
steps.body: Factors: physical (size, grade, mode of occurrence) and economic (demand, technology, capital, labour, transport). Methods: **surface/open-cast** — cheapest, for minerals near surface; **underground/shaft** — vertical shafts, needs lifts, ventilation; risky (fires, floods, gases). Developed countries are retreating from mining due to high labour costs; developing countries depend on mineral exports.

steps.title: Solved: why low yield per acre on Prairies?
steps.body: Extensive farming spreads limited inputs over huge areas with low rainfall; the aim is high output per worker, not per hectare.

steps.title: Solved: truck farming arithmetic
steps.body: If a truck averages 60 km/h for 8 hours overnight → 480 km market radius.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Kolkhoz = collective farming (USSR), not cooperative.

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **महादेवी वर्मा** (1907–1987) छायावाद की प्रमुख कवयित्री और श्रेष्ठ गद्यकार। 'स्मृति की रेखाएँ', 'अतीत के चलचित्र' में उनके संस्मरणात्मक रेखाचित्र हैं। ज्ञानपीठ (यामा), पद्म विभूषण।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
भक्तिन का असली नाम **लछमिन (लक्ष्मी)** था, पर जीवन में समृद्धि नहीं थी, इसलिए वह यह नाम छिपाती थी। वह **झूँसी** गाँव के एक गोपालक की बेटी थी; बचपन में माँ मर गई, विमाता ने कष्ट दिए, बहुत छोटी उम्र में विवाह हुआ। तीन बेटियाँ होने पर सास और जिठानियों ने उसका तिरस्कार किया, क्योंकि वे बेटों की माँ थीं। पति का साथ अच्छा था, पर वह जल्दी मर गया।

जेठ-जिठौत संपत्ति हड़पना चाहते थे; भक्तिन ने हार नहीं मानी, सिर मुँड़ाकर खेती सँभाली। बड़ी बेटी विधवा हुई, तो एक जिठौत ने ज़बरदस्ती की और **पंचायत** ने अन्यायपूर्ण फ़ैसला दिया। लगान न चुका पाने और अपमान के बाद भक्तिन शहर आकर लेखिका की सेविका बनी। वह लेखिका को अपने देहाती ढंग में ढाल लेती, झूठ को 'सही' बनाने के लिए तर्क गढ़ती, पैसे छिपाती ('रुपया-पैसा सँभालना'), पर लेखिका के लिए जान देने को तैयार। युद्ध के समय भी, और लेखिका के जेल जाने की बात पर भी वह साथ रहने को तत्पर थी।

steps.body:

steps.title: वाक्य-प्रयोग
steps.body:

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:
- भक्तिन लेखिका की रिश्तेदार नहीं, सेविका थी।
- भक्तिन ने लेखिका को नहीं बदला, लेखिका स्वयं भक्तिन के ढंग में ढल गईं — यह व्यंग्य-विनोद है।
- 'जिठौत' = जेठ का बेटा, 'जेठ' नहीं।

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: महादेवी भक्तिन के व्यक्तित्व के दोनों पक्ष ईमानदारी से दिखाती हैं — उसकी कमियाँ (झूठ को सही ठहराना, शास्त्र का अपने अनुसार अर्थ लगाना, पैसे छिपाना) और गुण (कर्मठता, स्वाभिमान, अटूट निष्ठा)। भक्तिन का जीवन बताता है कि भारतीय ग्रामीण समाज में स्त्री, विशेषकर विधवा और बेटियों की माँ, किस तरह शोषित होती थी। फिर भी वह हारती नहीं — यही उसकी महानता है।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: आज भी बेटे-बेटी में भेद, संपत्ति में बेटियों का हक़ न देना, और जाति/खाप पंचायतों के अन्यायपूर्ण फ़ैसले समाचारों में दिखते हैं। क़ानूनन बेटियों को पैतृक संपत्ति में बराबर अधिकार है (हिंदू उत्तराधिकार संशोधन 2005)।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** भक्तिन अपना वास्तविक नाम लोगों से क्यों छुपाती थी?
**उत्तर:** उसका नाम लक्ष्मी (समृद्धि की देवी) था, जबकि वह जीवन भर गरीबी और दुःख में रही। नाम और जीवन के इस विरोधाभास के कारण लोग हँसते, इसलिए वह नाम छिपाती थी।

**प्रश्न:** भक्तिन द्वारा शास्त्र के प्रश्न को सुविधा से सुलझा लेने का क्या उदाहरण लेखिका ने दिया है?
**उत्तर:** लेखिका ने सिर मुँड़ाने से मना किया तो भक्तिन ने कहा — 'तीरथ गए मुँड़ाए सिद्ध' — यानी शास्त्र में लिखा है। इस अधूरी उक्ति से उसने अपनी बात सही ठहरा दी।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:
**लोकोक्ति/मुहावरे (पाठ से)**: 'तीरथ गए मुँड़ाए सिद्ध'; 'आँखों में धूल झोंकना' = धोखा देना।

**शब्द-निर्माण**: वि + माता = विमाता; तिरस् + कार = तिरस्कार; भक्त + इन = भक्तिन (स्त्रीलिंग प्रत्यय 'इन')।

steps.title: उत्तर लिखने की युक्ति
steps.body:
- पहले प्रश्न का मुख्य शब्द पहचानें।
- पाठ से एक घटना या पंक्ति का उदाहरण दें।
- छोटे प्रश्न में 3–4 वाक्य, बड़े प्रश्न में 6–7 वाक्य लिखें।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **जैनेंद्र कुमार** (1905–1988) मनोवैज्ञानिक कथाकार और विचारक। 'त्यागपत्र', 'सुनीता' उपन्यास प्रसिद्ध। उनके निबंधों में दार्शनिकता और सरल संवाद-शैली है।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
लेखक के एक मित्र बाज़ार गए और ढेर सामान ले आए। लेखक कहते हैं कि यह **'पर्चेज़िंग पावर'** (क्रय-शक्ति) का घमंड है। बाज़ार का **जादू** आँखों के रास्ते काम करता है — जब **जेब भरी हो और मन ख़ाली** हो, तब यह सबसे ज़्यादा असर करता है; हम अनावश्यक चीज़ें ख़रीद लेते हैं, जो बाद में आराम नहीं, खलल देती हैं। उपाय: मन ख़ाली लेकर बाज़ार न जाएँ — **लक्ष्य** स्पष्ट हो। पर मन को बंद कर लेना (शून्य होना) भी ठीक नहीं; वह हठयोग है।

दूसरे मित्र ख़ाली हाथ लौटे — सब कुछ ख़रीदना चाहते थे, तो कुछ न ले सके। फिर **भगत जी** का उदाहरण: वे चूरन बेचते हैं, **छह आने** की कमाई होते ही बाक़ी चूरन बच्चों को मुफ़्त बाँट देते हैं। बाज़ार में वे केवल ज़रूरी चीज़ (जीरा, काला नमक) लेते हैं; बाज़ार का जादू उन पर नहीं चलता। ऐसे लोग बाज़ार को **सार्थकता** देते हैं। जो दिखावे के लिए ख़रीदते हैं, वे बाज़ार को **शैतानी शक्ति** बनाते हैं — **कपट** बढ़ता है, सद्भाव घटता है, ग्राहक-दुकानदार एक-दूसरे को ठगने लगते हैं। यही 'बाज़ारूपन' है।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
सूखे के दिनों में गाँव के 10–12 वर्ष के लड़के **इंदर सेना** (लेखक के साथी उन्हें 'मेढक-मंडली' कहते) बनाकर घर-घर जाते, कीचड़ में लोटते और 'काले मेघा पानी दे' गाते। लोग उन पर बाल्टियाँ भर पानी डालते। लेखक (तब किशोर, आर्यसमाजी विचारों वाले) इसे **अंधविश्वास** और पानी की बर्बादी मानते थे।

लेखक की **जीजी** (मुँहबोली बहन) उनसे बहुत प्रेम करती थीं; वे पूजा-अनुष्ठान लेखक से करवातीं। एक बार लेखक ने इंदर सेना पर पानी डालने से मना कर दिया। जीजी ने समझाया — यह पानी की बर्बादी नहीं, **'अर्घ्य'** (दान) है। जो चीज़ हमें दुर्लभ है, उसका दान करो, तभी फल मिलता है; **त्याग** के बिना दान नहीं। किसान भी पहले गेहूँ के बीज (पाँच-छह सेर) बोता है, तब फसल पाता है — 'यदि तुम पहले बोओगे नहीं तो काटोगे क्या?'

लेखक अंत में देश की स्थिति पर व्यंग्य करते हैं — आज़ादी के बाद हम त्याग की बात करते हैं, पर भ्रष्टाचार में डूबे हैं; करोड़ों की योजनाएँ हैं, पर 'गगरी फूटी की फूटी' रह जाती है।

steps.body: पाठ आस्था और विज्ञान के बीच संवाद है। लेखक का किशोर मन तर्क देता है — पानी की कमी में उसे फेंकना मूर्खता है। जीजी का लोक-ज्ञान कहता है — दुर्लभ वस्तु का त्याग ही सच्चा दान है, और प्रकृति से पाने के लिए पहले देना पड़ता है। लेखक अंत में इस त्याग-दर्शन को देश पर लागू करते हैं — हम केवल माँगते हैं, देते नहीं; भ्रष्टाचार से योजनाओं का लाभ लोगों तक नहीं पहुँचता।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** जीजी ने इंदर सेना पर पानी फेंके जाने को किस तरह सही ठहराया?
**उत्तर:** जीजी ने कहा — यह पानी की बर्बादी नहीं, इंद्र को अर्घ्य है। जो चीज़ हमारे पास कम है उसी का त्याग सच्चा दान है। जैसे किसान पहले बीज बोता है तब फसल पाता है, वैसे ही पानी देंगे तो पानी मिलेगा।

**प्रश्न:** 'काले मेघा पानी दे' संस्मरण में लेखक ने लोक-प्रचलित विश्वास और विज्ञान के द्वंद्व का चित्रण किया है। आप इस संबंध में क्या सोचते हैं?
**उत्तर:** विज्ञान तर्क देता है कि पानी फेंकने से वर्षा नहीं होती; पर लोक-विश्वास के पीछे त्याग, सामूहिकता और आशा का भाव है। हमें अंधविश्वास से बचते हुए उसके सकारात्मक मूल्य (त्याग, सहयोग) अपनाने चाहिए।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:
**लोकगीत की पंक्ति**: 'काले मेघा पानी दे, गगरी फूटी बैल पियासा' — देशज शब्द (पियासा = प्यासा)।

**संधि**: उत् + आसीन = उदासीन (व्यंजन संधि)।

**मुहावरे**: 'पानी फेरना' = नष्ट करना; 'गगरी फूटना' = साधन नष्ट होना।

- पाठ से एक घटना या पंक्ति का उदाहरण दें।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **फणीश्वरनाथ रेणु** (1921–1977) आंचलिक कथा-साहित्य के प्रमुख लेखक; बिहार के पूर्णिया (अब अररिया) ज़िले से। 'मैला आँचल', 'परती परिकथा' उपन्यास; 'मारे गए गुलफ़ाम' (तीसरी कसम) कहानी। पद्मश्री।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
**लुट्टन सिंह** नौ वर्ष की उम्र में अनाथ हो गया; विधवा सास ने पाला। गाय चराते, दूध पीते, कसरत करते वह पहलवान बना। **श्यामनगर** के दंगल में उसने प्रसिद्ध पहलवान **चाँद सिंह ('शेर के बच्चे')** को ललकारा। राजा साहब ने रोका, पर लुट्टन ने **ढोल की थाप** को गुरु मानकर दाँव लगाए — 'चट्-गिड़-धा' = 'मत डरना', 'धाक-धिना' = 'दाँव काटो' — और जीत गया। राजा साहब ने उसे **राज-पहलवान** बना लिया।

पंद्रह वर्ष तक वह अजेय रहा; उसके दो बेटे भी पहलवान बने। राजा साहब की मृत्यु के बाद विलायत से लौटे **राजकुमार** ने पहलवानी को फ़िज़ूलख़र्च मानकर उसे निकाल दिया। लुट्टन गाँव लौट आया, बच्चों को कुश्ती सिखाने लगा। फिर गाँव में **मलेरिया-हैज़ा** फैला; रोज़ लोग मरते। रात भर लुट्टन ढोलक बजाता, जिससे मरते लोगों को हिम्मत मिलती। एक दिन उसके दोनों बेटे मर गए; उस रात भी उसने ढोलक बजाई। कुछ दिन बाद ढोलक नहीं बजी — लुट्टन मर चुका था; उसे **पेट के बल चिता पर** लिटाया गया, और ढोलक बजाई गई।

**प्रश्न:** कुश्ती के समय ढोल की आवाज़ और लुट्टन के दाँव-पेंच में क्या तालमेल था?
**उत्तर:** ढोल की हर थाप लुट्टन को एक संदेश देती थी — 'चट्-धा, गिड़-धा' = 'आ जा, भिड़ जा'; 'चटाक्-चट्-धा' = 'उठाकर पटक दे'; 'धाक-धिना, तिरकट-तिना' = 'दाँव काटो, बाहर हो जाओ'। वह ढोल की लय पर दाँव लगाता था।

**प्रश्न:** महामारी फैलने के बाद गाँव में सूर्योदय और सूर्यास्त के दृश्य में क्या अंतर होता था?
**उत्तर:** सूर्योदय होने पर लोग रोते-कलपते भी अपने रोगी स्वजनों की देखभाल में लगते, थोड़ी चहल-पहल रहती; सूर्यास्त होते ही लोग घरों में दुबक जाते, गाँव पर सन्नाटा छा जाता, केवल ढोलक की आवाज़ सुनाई देती।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
लेखक जेठ की तपती गर्मी में **शिरीष** के फूलों को देखते हैं — जब सब कुछ झुलस रहा है, वह वसंत से भादों तक फूलता रहता है। वह **कालजयी अवधूत** की तरह है — सुख-दुःख में अविचलित। शिरीष के फूल बहुत **कोमल** होते हैं — संस्कृत साहित्य में (कालिदास) उन्हें कोमलता का प्रतीक माना गया — पर उसके **फल** बहुत मज़बूत होते हैं; नए फल आने तक पुराने फल डटे रहते हैं, खड़खड़ाते रहते हैं। लेखक इसकी तुलना उन **नेताओं/बुज़ुर्गों** से करते हैं जो नई पीढ़ी को जगह नहीं देते, जबकि **जीर्ण** और **जड़** को जाना ही है — 'महाकाल देवता' सबको झाड़ता है।

कालिदास अनासक्त योगी जैसे कवि थे, इसलिए शकुंतला का सौंदर्य-वर्णन कर सके। लेखक कहते हैं — शिरीष वायुमंडल से रस खींचकर जीता है, वैसे ही अवधूत बाहरी परिस्थितियों से अप्रभावित रहता है। आधुनिक युग में **गांधीजी** ऐसे ही अवधूत थे — हिंसा, अग्निकांड, मार-काट के बीच भी स्थिर।

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: द्विवेदी जी प्रकृति से दर्शन निकालते हैं। शिरीष भीषण गर्मी में खिलता है क्योंकि वह भीतर से रस खींचता है — बाहरी परिस्थितियाँ उसे नहीं हरा सकतीं। यह स्थितप्रज्ञता (गीता) का प्रतीक है। पुराने फलों का न झड़ना उस मानसिकता पर व्यंग्य है जो समय रहते जगह नहीं छोड़ती। 'जो कवि अनासक्त नहीं रह सका… वह कवि नहीं' — कालिदास का उदाहरण कला में तटस्थता का महत्त्व बताता है।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** लेखक ने शिरीष को कालजयी अवधूत की तरह क्यों माना है?
**उत्तर:** जैसे अवधूत सुख-दुःख, सर्दी-गर्मी में समान रहता है, वैसे ही शिरीष भीषण गर्मी, लू और सूखे में भी फूलों से लदा रहता है। वह समय की मार को झेलकर भी अविचलित रहता है, इसलिए कालजयी अवधूत है।

**प्रश्न:** 'हाय, वह अवधूत आज कहाँ है!' — ऐसा कहकर लेखक ने आत्मबल पर देह-बल के वर्चस्व की वर्तमान सभ्यता के संकट की ओर संकेत किया है। कैसे?
**उत्तर:** लेखक गांधीजी जैसे अवधूत को याद करते हैं जो आत्मबल से हिंसा का सामना करते थे। आज की सभ्यता शक्ति, हथियार और भौतिक बल पर टिकी है; आत्मबल और नैतिकता का अभाव ही वर्तमान संकट है।

**उपसर्ग**: अन् + आसक्त = अनासक्त; दुर् + अंत = दुरंत।

**समास**: कालजयी (काल को जीतने वाला — तत्पुरुष); महाकाल (कर्मधारय)।

steps.title: रचनाकार परिचय
steps.body: **डॉ. भीमराव आंबेडकर** (1891–1956) भारतीय संविधान की प्रारूप समिति के अध्यक्ष, विधिवेत्ता, अर्थशास्त्री, समाज-सुधारक। यह पाठ उनके प्रसिद्ध भाषण 'जाति का उच्छेद' (Annihilation of Caste, 1936) पर आधारित है। 1990 में मरणोपरांत भारत रत्न।

steps.title: पाठ का सारांश
steps.body:
**श्रम-विभाजन और जाति-प्रथा**: कुछ लोग कहते हैं कि जाति-प्रथा श्रम-विभाजन का ही रूप है, जो आधुनिक समाज के लिए ज़रूरी है। आंबेडकर कहते हैं — श्रम-विभाजन तो ठीक है, पर जाति-प्रथा **श्रमिकों का विभाजन** करती है, और ये विभाजित वर्ग एक-दूसरे से **ऊँच-नीच** में बँटे हैं। यह विभाजन **रुचि या क्षमता** पर नहीं, **जन्म** (माता-पिता की सामाजिक स्थिति) पर आधारित है। व्यक्ति को पेशा बदलने की अनुमति नहीं, भले ही भूखों मरना पड़े — इससे **बेरोज़गारी** बढ़ती है, क्योंकि तकनीक बदलने पर पुराने पेशे ख़त्म होते हैं। अरुचि से किया काम कुशलता नहीं लाता। अतः जाति-प्रथा आर्थिक दृष्टि से भी हानिकारक है।

**मेरी कल्पना का आदर्श समाज**: ऐसा समाज जो **स्वतंत्रता, समता और भ्रातृता** पर आधारित हो। उसमें गतिशीलता हो, बदलाव समाज के हर हिस्से तक पहुँचे, सबकी भागीदारी हो — यही **लोकतंत्र** है, जो केवल शासन-पद्धति नहीं, **सामूहिक जीवनचर्या** है। समता क्यों? क्योंकि जन्म, परिवार, शिक्षा के अवसर सबको समान नहीं मिलते; इसलिए समाज को सबके साथ **समान व्यवहार** करना चाहिए।

steps.title: मुख्य बिंदु
steps.body:
- जाति-प्रथा = श्रमिकों का अस्वाभाविक विभाजन
- जन्म-आधारित पेशा → बेरोज़गारी, अकुशलता

- लोकतंत्र = सामूहिक जीवनचर्या

steps.title: विस्तृत व्याख्या
steps.body: आंबेडकर तर्क और तथ्य से बात रखते हैं। आर्थिक तर्क: पेशा बदलने की आज़ादी न हो तो तकनीकी बदलाव में लोग बेरोज़गार हो जाते हैं। मनोवैज्ञानिक तर्क: अरुचि से किया काम कुशलता नहीं देता। नैतिक तर्क: जन्म से किसी को ऊँचा-नीचा मानना अन्याय है। समता के पक्ष में उनका व्यावहारिक तर्क है — भले ही सबकी क्षमताएँ समान न हों, पर शुरुआती असमानताएँ (जन्म, परिवार, शिक्षा) व्यक्ति के हाथ में नहीं, इसलिए समाज को सबके साथ समान व्यवहार करना चाहिए।

steps.title: आज के जीवन से जोड़ें
steps.body: भारतीय संविधान के अनुच्छेद 14–17 (समानता, भेदभाव निषेध, अस्पृश्यता उन्मूलन) और अनुच्छेद 19(1)(g) (कोई भी पेशा अपनाने की स्वतंत्रता) इन्हीं विचारों पर आधारित हैं। आज करियर का चुनाव रुचि और योग्यता से होना चाहिए।

steps.title: प्रश्न-उत्तर (हल सहित)
steps.body:
**प्रश्न:** जाति-प्रथा को श्रम-विभाजन का ही एक रूप न मानने के पीछे आंबेडकर के क्या तर्क हैं?
**उत्तर:** (1) यह श्रम का नहीं, श्रमिकों का विभाजन है; (2) विभाजित वर्ग ऊँच-नीच में बँटे हैं; (3) विभाजन जन्म पर आधारित है, रुचि या क्षमता पर नहीं; (4) पेशा बदलने की अनुमति नहीं, जिससे बेरोज़गारी होती है।

**प्रश्न:** लेखक ने 'आदर्श समाज' में किन बातों को ज़रूरी माना है?
**उत्तर:** स्वतंत्रता, समता और भ्रातृता; समाज में गतिशीलता ताकि बदलाव हर हिस्से तक पहुँचे; सबकी सामूहिक भागीदारी; और लोकतंत्र को सामूहिक जीवनचर्या के रूप में अपनाना।

steps.title: व्याकरण बिंदु
steps.body:
**उपसर्ग**: अ + परिहार्य = अपरिहार्य; अ + स्वाभाविक = अस्वाभाविक; उत् + छेद = उच्छेद।

**भाववाचक संज्ञा**: समता (सम + ता), भ्रातृता (भ्रातृ + ता), स्वतंत्रता (स्वतंत्र + ता)।

steps.title: उत्तर लिखने की युक्ति
steps.body:
- पहले प्रश्न का मुख्य शब्द पहचानें।
- पाठ से एक घटना या पंक्ति का उदाहरण दें।
- छोटे प्रश्न में 3–4 वाक्य, बड़े प्रश्न में 6–7 वाक्य लिखें।

steps.body: काव्य पढ़ने/सुनने से मिलने वाला आनंद **रस** है। अंग: **स्थायी भाव**, **विभाव** (आलंबन, उद्दीपन), **अनुभाव**, **संचारी (व्यभिचारी) भाव** — कुल 33 संचारी भाव माने गए हैं।

steps.title: आम गलतियाँ
steps.body:

steps.title: छंद
steps.body: मात्रा/वर्ण की संख्या, क्रम, यति और गति के नियमों से बँधी रचना **छंद** है। **लघु (।)** = 1 मात्रा (अ, इ, उ, ऋ और इनकी मात्राएँ); **गुरु (ऽ)** = 2 मात्राएँ (आ, ई, ऊ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ; अनुस्वार/विसर्ग युक्त; संयुक्ताक्षर से पहले का वर्ण)।

steps.body: क्या, कौन, कहाँ, कब, क्यों, कैसे — अच्छे समाचार में इन सबका उत्तर हो।

steps.body: सबसे महत्त्वपूर्ण बात (**इंट्रो/मुखड़ा**) पहले, फिर **बॉडी** (विवरण), अंत में **समापन** (कम महत्त्व की बातें)। इससे जगह कम होने पर नीचे से काटा जा सकता है।

school-c12-history.description: Chapter courses for the first part of Class 12 Indian history: the Harappan civilisation, early states and economies, kinship and caste in the Mahabharata, and Buddhist, Jaina and Puranic traditions — with source-based and map practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation
courses.summary: The Harappan (Indus Valley) civilisation: subsistence, town planning at Mohenjodaro, craft production, trade, seals and script, possible authority, decline, and how archaeologists discovered and interpret it.
outcomes: Learners can describe Harappan town planning with examples
Learners can explain craft production and trade networks with sites
Learners can discuss the script, seals and theories of authority and decline
Learners can trace the history of discovery (Sahni, Banerji, Marshall, Wheeler)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: About 4,500 years ago, a trader walks along a straight brick street; covered drains run beside him.
On the raised Citadel stands the Great Bath, sealed with bitumen.

steps.title: Where and when
steps.body: Mature Harappan phase: **c. 2600–1900 BCE**. Sites spread across modern Pakistan and north-west India: **Harappa** (Punjab, Pakistan, on the Ravi), **Mohenjodaro** (Sindh, on the Indus), **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan), **Lothal** and **Dholavira** (Gujarat), **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana), **Banawali** (Haryana), **Shortughai** (Afghanistan, far north).

steps.title: Subsistence
steps.body: Wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame; millets in Gujarat; rice rarely. Animal bones: cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo, pig; also fish and wild animals. Evidence of ploughing: terracotta plough models (Cholistan, **Banawali**) and a **ploughed field at Kalibangan** with two crops grown together. Irrigation: canals at Shortughai, reservoirs at Dholavira.

steps.title: Mohenjodaro's plan
steps.body:
- **Citadel**: smaller, higher, on mud-brick platforms — warehouse, **Great Bath**.
- **Lower Town**: residential, walled, streets on an approximate **grid**.
- **Drains**: every house connected to street drains; planned before houses were built.
- Houses: courtyard, no windows on ground-floor walls facing street, private bathing areas, some with wells (about 700 wells counted).
- Standard bricks in ratio **1:2:4**.

steps.title: Solved: evidence of planning
steps.body: **Q:** Give three features showing planning. **A:** 1) Settlement planned first, platforms built before houses. 2) Standardised bricks (1:2:4) across sites. 3) Drainage laid out with streets. 4) Grid-like layout.

steps.title: Solved: brick arithmetic
steps.body: A brick ratio 1:2:4 with thickness 7 cm → width 14 cm, length 28 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Great Bath is on the **Citadel**, not Lower Town.
- Do not say Harappans grew mainly rice — wheat and barley dominated.

scenes.text: In Chanhudaro, craftsmen drill carnelian beads with fine tools.
Far away, Mesopotamian texts mention ships from 'Meluhha'.

steps.title: Craft production
steps.body: **Chanhudaro** was almost entirely devoted to crafts: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making, weight-making. Beads from carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz, steatite, copper, bronze, gold, shell, faience. Shell work at **Nageshwar** and **Balakot**. Archaeologists identify craft centres by **raw material, tools, unfinished objects and waste**.

steps.title: Procuring materials
steps.body:
- Settlements in raw-material areas: Nageshwar/Balakot (shell), **Shortughai** (lapis lazuli), Lothal (carnelian, steatite).
- Expeditions: **Khetri** (Rajasthan) for copper; south India for gold.
- Long distance: copper from **Oman** (Magan); Mesopotamian texts mention **Meluhha** (probably Harappan region), and Dilmun (Bahrain).

steps.title: Seals, weights, script
steps.body: Seals (often steatite) with animal motifs and signs were used to stamp clay on bags — sealing for trade. The **script is undeciphered**; it had about 375–400 signs, written **right to left**, not alphabetic. **Weights**: cubical chert, binary (1, 2, 4, 8…16, 32…) then decimal for higher values.

steps.title: Solved: how is Meluhha linked to Harappa?
steps.body: 1) Mesopotamian texts list carnelian, lapis, copper, gold and woods from Meluhha. 2) These match Harappan products. 3) A Harappan-style seal and weights found in the Gulf region. So Meluhha very probably referred to the Harappan region.

steps.title: Solved: weights
steps.body: Binary series: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. The 6th weight in the series = 2⁵ = **32** units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Never write 'the script has been deciphered'.
- Seals were not coins.

scenes.text: In 1924, John Marshall announces a new civilisation to the world.
Decades later, archaeologists debate who ruled and why the cities declined.

steps.title: Who ruled?
steps.body: Uniformity in bricks, weights, seals and planning suggests **some central authority**. Theories: priest-kings (based on a statue labelled 'priest-king' — a name borrowed from Mesopotamian ideas, not proven); several rulers in different cities; or a single state. No clear palace or temple.

steps.title: End of the civilisation
steps.body: By about **1900 BCE** most mature sites were abandoned or changed: fewer seals, script use ended, long-distance trade declined. Explanations: climate change, deforestation, floods, river shifts or drying, overuse of land. A single cause like an 'Aryan invasion' is rejected by archaeologists — the skeletons at Mohenjodaro (cited by Wheeler) did not belong to one period.

steps.title: Discovery
steps.body:
- **Alexander Cunningham**, first Director-General of the ASI (19th century), noticed seals but missed the significance.
- **Daya Ram Sahni** found seals at Harappa (1921); **Rakhal Das Banerji** at Mohenjodaro (1922).
- **John Marshall** announced a new civilisation (**1924**).
- **R.E.M. Wheeler** (1944) introduced stratigraphic methods.

steps.title: Solved: problems of interpretation
steps.body: 1) Script unreadable, so artefacts are interpreted without texts. 2) Archaeologists classify objects by material and function. 3) Religious practices are reconstructed from seals ('proto-Shiva' seal) and terracotta 'mother goddess' figurines — guesses based on later traditions.

steps.title: Solved: time gap
steps.body: Seals found 1921; announcement 1924 → 3 years later. Wheeler's work 1944 = 20 years after Marshall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Priest-king' is a label, not a proven title.

scenes.text: James Prinsep, an officer of the East India Company mint, deciphers Brahmi and Kharosthi.
Suddenly many rock edicts name a king 'Piyadassi' — later identified as Ashoka.

steps.title: Inscriptions
steps.body: Writings engraved on stone, metal or pottery; they record achievements, donations, orders. **Brahmi** (most Ashokan edicts) and **Kharosthi** (north-west) were deciphered by **James Prinsep (1838)**. Limits: letters faint/damaged, meanings uncertain, they reflect the views of those who commissioned them, routine life rarely recorded.

steps.title: Sixteen mahajanapadas (6th c. BCE)
steps.body: Buddhist and Jaina texts list sixteen 'great states' — e.g. **Vajji, Magadha, Koshala, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara, Avanti**. Most were ruled by kings; some like Vajji were **ganas/sanghas** ruled by groups. Each had a fortified capital. Dharmasutras laid down norms for rulers (ideally kshatriyas) to collect taxes and tribute.

steps.title: Why Magadha rose
steps.body:
- Fertile Ganga valley; abundant **iron** mines (present-day Jharkhand).
- **Elephants** from forests for the army.
- Ganga and tributaries for communication.
- Ambitious rulers: **Bimbisara, Ajatasattu, Mahapadma Nanda**.
- Capital moved from **Rajagaha** (Rajgir, hill-fort) to **Pataliputra** (Patna, on rivers) in the 4th c. BCE.

steps.title: Solved: limits of epigraphy
steps.body: 1) Damaged letters. 2) Uncertain word meanings. 3) Many inscriptions not yet deciphered/published. 4) Propaganda of rulers. 5) Little about ordinary routine life.

steps.title: Solved: Rajagaha vs Pataliputra
steps.body: Rajagaha was a fortified settlement among hills — defensive. Pataliputra sat at the confluence of rivers — better communication and trade. The move signals expansion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in **1838**, not Harappan script.

lessons.title: The Mauryan empire and Ashoka's dhamma

scenes.text: Ashoka's army conquers Kalinga; an inscription speaks of his remorse.
He orders his message of dhamma carved on rocks and pillars across the empire.

steps.title: Founding and sources
steps.body: **Chandragupta Maurya** founded the empire about **321 BCE**, extending to Afghanistan and Baluchistan. Grandson **Ashoka** conquered **Kalinga** (coastal Odisha). Sources: archaeology (Sarnath lion capital), **Megasthenes' Indica** (Greek ambassador; fragments survive), **Arthashastra** (parts by Kautilya/Chanakya), later Buddhist/Jaina/Puranic texts, Ashoka's inscriptions.

steps.title: Administration
steps.body: Five major political centres: capital **Pataliputra**, provincial centres **Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali, Suvarnagiri**. Megasthenes mentions a committee of 30 with six subcommittees (navy, transport, infantry, horses, chariots, elephants). Ashoka appointed **dhamma mahamattas** to spread dhamma.

steps.title: Dhamma
steps.body: Ashoka's dhamma = ethical principles: respect for elders, generosity to brahmanas and renouncers, kind treatment of slaves and servants, respect for all sects, non-violence. It was not imposing Buddhism as state religion.

steps.title: Solved: was the Mauryan empire uniform?
steps.body: No: core around Magadha was tightly controlled; provincial centres like Taxila and Ujjayini had important routes; forest regions were loosely controlled. Diverse terrain (Afghan hills to Odisha coast) prevented uniform administration.

steps.title: Solved: subcommittees
steps.body: Committee of 30 ÷ 6 subcommittees = 5 members each.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dhamma ≠ 'Dharma of Buddhism only'. Ashoka's inscriptions are mostly in **Prakrit** in Brahmi; in the north-west Kharosthi, and in Afghanistan Greek and Aramaic.

lessons.title: Later kingdoms, farmers, towns and coins

scenes.text: Court poet Harishena carves a prashasti on the Allahabad pillar praising Samudragupta.
In villages, iron ploughshares and paddy transplantation increase yields.

steps.title: New notions of kingship
steps.body:
- **Kushanas** (c. 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE) claimed divinity: titles like *devaputra*; colossal statues at Mat (near Mathura).
- **Guptas** (4th c. CE): **prashastis** like Harishena's **Prayaga Prashasti** for **Samudragupta**.
- In the south, **chiefs and samantas** owed allegiance to rulers.

steps.title: Agrarian change
steps.body: Rising taxes made farmers increase output: **iron ploughshare** in fertile alluvial areas; **paddy transplantation** in the Ganga valley; **irrigation** through wells, tanks, canals. Inequality grew: large landowners (**gahapatis**, village headmen) vs landless labourers. **Land grants** (from c. 1st c. CE), e.g. to brahmanas (**agrahara**), recorded on copper plates.

steps.title: Towns, trade and coins
steps.body: Towns on rivers and routes: Pataliputra, Ujjayini, Puhar. Guilds (**shrenis**). Trade from central Asia to Rome via sea and land; spices, textiles, medicinal plants. **Punch-marked coins** (silver, copper — 6th c. BCE) first; **Indo-Greek** coins with ruler images; **Kushanas** issued the first large-scale **gold coins**; **Yaudheyas** (tribal republic) issued copper coins; **Guptas** issued remarkable gold coins.

steps.title: Solved: why land grants?
steps.body: Explanations: extend agriculture to new lands; rulers sought allies; weakening kings granted land to gain support; spread brahmanical culture. Historians debate — evaluate several.

steps.title: Solved: coin evidence
steps.body: Yaudheya copper coins show a tribal republic minted money — evidence of their interest in exchange. Roman coins in south India show trade with Rome.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: First gold coins on a large scale were Kushana, not Mauryan.

lessons.title: The Mahabharata critical edition and families

scenes.text: In 1919 scholars led by V.S. Sukthankar begin collecting Mahabharata manuscripts from all over India.
Forty-seven years later, the critical edition is complete.

steps.title: Critical edition
steps.body: The project began in **1919** under **V.S. Sukthankar** at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune. Scholars compared Sanskrit manuscripts in many scripts, selected verses common to most, and completed the work in **1966** (over 13,000 pages). Findings: a common core across regions, and many **regional variations** — showing the text grew through dialogue between dominant traditions and local ones.

steps.title: Families and patriliny
steps.body: **Kula** (family) and **jnati** (larger kin network). **Patriliny**: descent traced from father to son, grandson. Mahabharata's core story is a feud over land and power between cousins (Kauravas and Pandavas), both of the Kuru lineage — reinforcing patrilineal succession. Exceptions: sometimes brothers succeeded; rarely women (e.g. Prabhavati Gupta).

steps.title: Solved: why is the epic a 'dynamic text'?
steps.body: 1) Retold over centuries in many languages. 2) Local stories and characters added. 3) Performed in plays, dance, storytelling. So it is not fixed; regional versions differ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The critical edition was prepared in **Pune**, not Varanasi or Kolkata.

lessons.title: Marriage rules, gotra and the Satavahana exception

scenes.text: Satavahana kings call themselves 'Gotami-puta' — son of Gotami.
Why would kings be identified by their mothers?

steps.title: Rules of marriage
steps.body: Brahmanical texts (**Dharmasutras, Dharmashastras**, compiled c. 500 BCE onwards; **Manusmriti** c. 200 BCE–200 CE) prescribed norms. **Exogamy** (marrying outside the kin group) was preferred for daughters among high-status families. **Endogamy** = within a unit. **Polygyny** (a man with several wives) and **polyandry** (a woman with several husbands — Draupadi) both appear. Manusmriti lists **eight forms of marriage**, four considered good.

steps.title: Gotra
steps.body: From c. 1000 BCE, brahmanas classified people into **gotras** named after Vedic seers. Rules: women adopted the husband's gotra; members of the same gotra could not marry.

steps.title: The Satavahana case
steps.body: Satavahana rulers' names were derived from their mothers' gotra (e.g. Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani). Several queens retained their father's gotra (e.g. Gotama, Vasithi) rather than adopting the husband's. Some married within the same gotra — **endogamy**, common among south Indian communities. This shows norms were not universal.

steps.title: Solved: do metronymics mean matriliny?
steps.body: No — succession among Satavahanas was still **patrilineal** (father to son). The mother's name shows her importance, but power passed through sons.

steps.title: Solved: normative vs actual
steps.body: Normative texts (Manusmriti) tell us what authors wished; inscriptions and practices like the Satavahanas show what actually happened — historians compare both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not say 'Satavahanas were matrilineal' — they were patrilineal with metronymics.

scenes.text: A forest-dwelling boy, Ekalavya, learns archery on his own.

steps.title: Varna ideal
steps.body: Dharmasutras assigned occupations: **brahmanas** (study, teach Vedas, sacrifice), **kshatriyas** (war, protection, justice), **vaishyas** (agriculture, pastoralism, trade), **shudras** (serve the three). Strategies to enforce: divine origin claim (Purusha sukta), advising kings, persuading people that status was birth-based.

steps.title: Reality: not always kshatriya kings
steps.body: Many rulers were not kshatriyas: the Mauryas (Buddhist texts say kshatriyas, brahmanical texts low origin), **Shungas and Kanvas** were brahmanas, **Shakas** from Central Asia were seen as *mlechchhas*, yet Rudradaman repaired the Sudarshana lake. Satavahana Gotami-puta Siri-Satakani claimed to be a unique brahmana and destroyer of kshatriya pride, yet married into Shaka families. **Jatis** were numerous, often linked to occupation and organised in **shrenis**; forest people (nishadas) and **chandalas** were placed outside, considered 'untouchable' by texts — **Fa Xian** and **Xuan Zang** noted this.

steps.title: Property and gender
steps.body: Manusmriti: paternal estate divided equally among sons after parents' death; women could own **stridhana** (gifts at marriage) inherited by children. Women could not claim share of paternal resources. Wealthy women like **Prabhavati Gupta** (Vakataka queen) held land. **Gandhari's** advice to Duryodhana and Draupadi's question about Yudhishthira's right to stake her show women's voices in the epic.

steps.title: Solved: alternative views
steps.body: Buddhists rejected birth-based claims of superiority; a Buddhist text (Sutta Pitaka) argues kings should be chosen by the people (mahasammata) — a contrast to brahmanical divine order.

steps.title: Solved: case reading
steps.body: **Case:** A Shaka ruler repairs a famous lake in Gujarat. **Q:** What does it show? **A:** Foreigners regarded as mlechchhas could still adopt Sanskritic ideals of kingship and earn legitimacy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Varna ideals ≠ actual practice. Always contrast texts with evidence.

lessons.title: A time of questions: Jainism and Buddhism

scenes.text: Prince Siddhartha sees an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a renouncer.
Years later, meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he attains enlightenment and becomes the Buddha.

steps.title: Sixth century BCE ferment
steps.body: Thinkers debated the meaning of life, the afterlife and sacrifice. Upanishads explored atman and brahman. Many teachers — **Mahavira**, the **Buddha**, Makkhali Gosala (fatalist), Ajita Kesakambalin (materialist) — debated in **kutagarashalas** (huts with pointed roofs).

steps.title: Jainism
steps.body: Mahavira was the **24th tirthankara** (preceded by 23). Core idea: the entire world is animated; **ahimsa** (non-injury) to all beings. Cycle of birth and rebirth shaped by karma; liberation through renunciation and penance. Five vows: no killing, stealing, lying, possession, plus chastity. Jaina texts in Prakrit, later Sanskrit and Tamil.

steps.title: The Buddha's teaching
steps.body: The world is transient (**anicca**) and soulless (**anatta**); sorrow (**dukkha**) is intrinsic. Following the **middle path** between penance and indulgence leads to liberation; **nibbana** = extinguishing ego and desire. Teachings compiled in the **Tipitaka**: **Vinaya Pitaka** (rules for sangha), **Sutta Pitaka** (teachings), **Abhidhamma Pitaka** (philosophy).

steps.title: Solved: compare Jainism and Buddhism
steps.body: Similar: rejected Vedic sacrifices' authority, emphasised karma and liberation, used Prakrit/Pali, formed monastic orders. Different: Jainism stresses strict ahimsa and penance; Buddhism the middle path; Jainism believes in soul (jiva) in all things, Buddhism in anatta.

steps.title: Solved: three Pitakas
steps.body: Vinaya = rules; Sutta = teachings; Abhidhamma = philosophy. Mnemonic: **V-S-A: 'Very Simple Answers'**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mahavira did not found Jainism alone; he was the 24th tirthankara.

scenes.text: In the 19th–20th centuries, Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum fund the preservation of Sanchi.
Thanks partly to them, the stupa survives where it was built.

steps.title: The sangha
steps.body: The Buddha founded the **sangha** for monks (bhikkhus) who lived on alms. Women were admitted later — the Buddha's foster mother **Mahapajapati Gotami** was the first bhikkhuni, after his disciple Ananda's intervention. Members came from all social backgrounds; the sangha's internal decisions were by consensus or vote. **Therigatha** contains verses by bhikkhunis.

steps.title: Stupas
steps.body: Stupas enshrine **relics** (bodily remains or objects of the Buddha). Structure: **anda** (hemispherical mound), **harmika** (balcony-like structure on top), **yashti** (mast) with **chhatri** (umbrella), surrounded by a **railing** (vedika) and four ornamented **gateways (toranas)**. Donations recorded in inscriptions — from kings, guilds, ivory workers, monks, nuns, women.

steps.title: Sanchi and Amaravati
steps.body: **Sanchi** (near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh) survived intact; French and British wanted to take its gateways. **Amaravati** (Andhra Pradesh) was dismantled in the 19th century — sculptures removed to Calcutta, Madras and London. **H.H. Cole** argued for preserving antiquities in situ.

steps.title: Solved: why Sanchi survived
steps.body: 1) Rulers of Bhopal (Shahjehan Begum, Sultan Jehan Begum) funded preservation and publications. 2) John Marshall's volumes documented it. 3) It escaped the scholars and collectors who stripped Amaravati.

steps.title: Solved: label a stupa

steps.title: Common mistakes

lessons.title: Reading sculpture, Mahayana and Puranic traditions

scenes.text: A Sanchi relief shows an empty seat under a tree — but no Buddha figure.
Later, at Mathura and Gandhara, sculptors carve the Buddha in human form.

steps.title: Symbols at Sanchi
steps.body: Early art showed the Buddha through **symbols**: empty seat (meditation), **stupa** (mahaparinibbana), **wheel** (first sermon at Sarnath), tree (enlightenment). Other images: shalabhanjika (woman under tree — auspicious, from popular traditions), animals, nagas — showing Buddhism absorbed popular beliefs.

steps.title: Mahayana
steps.body: From the early centuries CE, **Mahayana** ('great vehicle') emphasised the Buddha as a saviour and **Bodhisattvas** — compassionate beings who postponed nibbana to help others. Buddha images made at **Mathura** and **Taxila/Gandhara**. Older tradition called **Hinayana** ('lesser vehicle') by Mahayanists; its followers called themselves **Theravada**.

steps.title: Puranic Hinduism and temples
steps.body: **Vaishnavism** (Vishnu; avataras — ten incarnations) and **Shaivism** (Shiva, often as linga). Puranas, composed by brahmanas, told stories in simple Sanskrit for all including women and shudras. Early temples: a square room (**garbhagriha**) with one doorway; later a tall **shikhara**, mandapas. Example: **Dashavatara temple at Deogarh** (UP, 5th c.); rock-cut **Kailashnatha** at Ellora (8th c.).

steps.title: Solved: why no Buddha image at first?
steps.body: Many early artists avoided showing the Buddha in human form; they used symbols to represent events. Historians interpret meanings using textual traditions — but must be cautious.

steps.title: Solved: Mahayana vs Theravada
steps.body: Mahayana: Bodhisattvas, Buddha images worshipped, saviour figure. Theravada: individual effort to attain nibbana, Buddha as a human teacher.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Hinayana' is a Mahayana term; Theravada is self-name.

scenes.text: Warden Rao lists which students share a room. 'Is a room-mate of' is a relation on the set of hostel students.
Is everyone their own room-mate? If A shares with B, does B share with A? These questions are exactly reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

steps.title: What is a relation?
steps.body:
A **relation R from A to B** is any subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R we write a R b. A relation **on A** is a subset of A × A.

- **Empty relation**: R = ∅ (no pair is related).
- **Universal relation**: R = A × A (every pair is related).

If |A| = n, then A × A has n² pairs, so the number of relations on A is 2^(n²).

steps.title: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive
steps.body:
For a relation R on A:

- **Reflexive**: (a, a) ∈ R for **every** a ∈ A.
- **Symmetric**: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R.
- **Transitive**: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.

To prove a property, argue for arbitrary elements. To disprove it, one counter-example is enough.

steps.title: Solved: R = {(a, b) : a ≤ b} on ℝ
steps.body:
Step 1 (reflexive): a ≤ a for all real a, so (a, a) ∈ R. ✔

Step 2 (symmetric): (1, 2) ∈ R since 1 ≤ 2, but 2 ≤ 1 is false, so (2, 1) ∉ R. ✘

Step 3 (transitive): a ≤ b and b ≤ c give a ≤ c. ✔

Conclusion: reflexive and transitive, **not** symmetric.

steps.title: Solved: R on A = {1, 2, 3}, R = {(1, 2), (2, 1)}
steps.body:
Step 1: (1, 1) ∉ R, so not reflexive.

Step 2: (1, 2) and (2, 1) both present, so symmetric. ✔

Step 3: (1, 2), (2, 1) ∈ R would need (1, 1) ∈ R for transitivity. It is missing, so **not transitive**.

Lesson: transitivity must be checked even when a = c.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive** is an **equivalence relation**.

The **equivalence class** of a is [a] = {x ∈ A : x R a}. Two classes are either identical or disjoint, and together they cover A — they form a **partition** of A.

steps.title: Solved: R = {(a, b): 3 divides a − b} on ℤ
steps.body:
Step 1: a − a = 0 is divisible by 3 ⇒ reflexive.

Step 2: if 3 | (a − b) then 3 | (b − a) = −(a − b) ⇒ symmetric.

Step 3: if 3 | (a − b) and 3 | (b − c), then 3 | [(a − b) + (b − c)] = a − c ⇒ transitive.

Hence an equivalence relation. Classes: [0] = {…, −3, 0, 3, 6, …}, [1] = {…, −2, 1, 4, …}, [2] = {…, −1, 2, 5, …}.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Let f : A → B.

- **One-one (injective)**: f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⇒ x₁ = x₂.
- **Onto (surjective)**: every y ∈ B has some x ∈ A with f(x) = y, i.e. range = codomain.
- **Bijective**: both one-one and onto.

For finite A and B with |A| = |B|, one-one ⇔ onto.

Onto: for any y, put x = (3 − y)/4 ∈ ℝ; then f(x) = y ✔.

Hence bijective.

steps.title: Invertible function

f : A → B is **invertible** if there is g : B → A with g∘f = I_A and f∘g = I_B. Then g = f⁻¹.

**Theorem**: f is invertible ⇔ f is bijective. Also (g∘f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.

steps.title: The idea
steps.body:
sin, cos, tan … are not one-one on ℝ (they repeat), so they have no inverse on ℝ. We **restrict the domain** to an interval where the function is one-one and onto its range, then invert.

sin⁻¹x means the angle in the principal branch whose sine is x. It is **not** 1/sin x.

steps.body:

Answer: −π/6.

steps.title: Solved: principal value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2)
steps.body:
Step 1: θ ∈ [0, π] with cos θ = −√3/2.

Step 2: cos(π/6) = √3/2; cos(π − θ) = −cos θ, so θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Answer: 5π/6 (not −π/6, which is outside [0, π]).

lessons.title: What a matrix is: order and types

scenes.text: Anu's stationery shop sells pens, pencils and erasers in two branches. She writes the stock as a 2 × 3 table.
That rectangular table of numbers is a matrix — and it lets her add, scale and multiply whole tables at once.

steps.title: Definition and order
steps.body: A **matrix** is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. A matrix with m rows and n columns has **order m × n** and mn elements. The element in row i, column j is written aᵢⱼ, and A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ.

steps.title: Types of matrices
steps.body:
- **Row matrix** 1 × n; **column matrix** m × 1.
- **Square matrix**: m = n. Its diagonal is a₁₁, a₂₂, …
- **Diagonal**: square, all off-diagonal entries 0.
- **Scalar**: diagonal with all diagonal entries equal.
- **Identity Iₙ**: scalar with diagonal entries 1.
- **Zero matrix O**: all entries 0.
- **Equal matrices**: same order and every corresponding entry equal.

steps.body: We need m × n = 12: 1×12, 12×1, 2×6, 6×2, 3×4, 4×3. **Six** possible orders. (With 7 elements — a prime — only 1×7 and 7×1.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing order as columns × rows. It is always **rows × columns**.
- Calling any square matrix with zeros 'diagonal' — the off-diagonal entries must all be 0.
- Comparing matrices of different orders for equality.

steps.title: Addition and scalar multiplication
steps.body:
For A, B of the **same order**, A + B = [aᵢⱼ + bᵢⱼ]. kA = [k·aᵢⱼ].

Properties: A + B = B + A, (A + B) + C = A + (B + C), k(A + B) = kA + kB, A + O = A.

steps.title: Multiplication
steps.body:
If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p with (AB)ᵢₖ = Σⱼ aᵢⱼ bⱼₖ (row i of A · column k of B).

Properties: (AB)C = A(BC), A(B + C) = AB + AC, AI = IA = A. In general **AB ≠ BA**, and AB = O does not force A = O or B = O.

steps.title: Solved: AB = O with non-zero matrices
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying entry-by-entry (that is not matrix multiplication).
- Expanding (A + B)² as A² + 2AB + B². Correct: A² + AB + BA + B² (equal only if AB = BA).
- Forgetting to check that columns of A = rows of B before multiplying.

steps.title: Real use
steps.body: Computer graphics rotate and scale images with matrix products; recommendation systems store user × item ratings as matrices.

steps.title: Transpose and its properties
steps.body:
A′ (or Aᵀ) is obtained by turning rows into columns: if A = [aᵢⱼ]ₘₓₙ, A′ = [aⱼᵢ]ₙₓₘ.

- (A′)′ = A
- (kA)′ = kA′
- (A + B)′ = A′ + B′
- **(AB)′ = B′A′** (order reverses)

steps.title: Symmetric and skew-symmetric
steps.body:
Square A is **symmetric** if A′ = A (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ), **skew-symmetric** if A′ = −A (aᵢⱼ = −aⱼᵢ; so every diagonal entry is 0).

**Theorem**: every square matrix is uniquely P + Q with P = ½(A + A′) symmetric and Q = ½(A − A′) skew-symmetric.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Putting non-zero diagonal entries in a skew-symmetric matrix.
- Forgetting the ½ in the decomposition.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A square matrix A is **invertible** if there is B with **AB = BA = I**. Then B = A⁻¹, and it is unique.

Properties: (A⁻¹)⁻¹ = A, (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹, (A′)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)′. A non-square matrix has no inverse.
