story.title: A number that judges a matrix

scenes.text: Every square matrix carries one special number — its determinant — that decides whether the matrix can be inverted.
Geometrically, a 2 × 2 determinant measures how much a shape's area is scaled by the matrix.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For A = [[a, b], [c, d]]: |A| = ad − bc.

For a 3 × 3 matrix, expand along any row or column using signs + − + / − + − / + − +:
|A| = a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁).

Only **square** matrices have determinants.

steps.title: Solved: |[[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 4], [5, 6, 0]]|
steps.body:
Expand along row 1:

1·(1·0 − 4·6) − 2·(0·0 − 4·5) + 3·(0·6 − 1·5) = −24 + 40 − 15 = **1**.

Tip: expanding along a row/column with most zeros saves time.

steps.title: Key results
steps.body:
- |A′| = |A|
- |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n × n matrix
- |AB| = |A||B|
- If two rows are identical (or proportional), |A| = 0

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the alternating sign on the middle term.
- Writing |3A| = 3|A| for a 3 × 3 matrix — it is 27|A|.
- Confusing determinant bars with absolute value (a determinant can be negative).

quiz.why: If two rows are equal, subtracting one from the other gives a zero row without changing the determinant, so |A| = 0.
For a diagonal matrix the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: 1 × 2 × 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Area of a triangle using determinants

scenes.text: A surveyor gives the corners of a triangular field as coordinates (1, 0), (6, 0) and (4, 3) in units of 10 m.
One determinant gives the area — and if it is zero, the three points are on a straight line.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
Area of triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃):

Δ = ½ |[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|, taking the **absolute value** of the result.

Three points are **collinear** ⇔ this determinant is 0.

steps.title: Solved: vertices (1, 0), (6, 0), (4, 3)
steps.body:
Expand: 1(0 − 3) − 0(6 − 4) + 1(18 − 0) = −3 + 18 = 15.

Δ = ½·15 = **7.5 square units**. With 1 unit = 10 m, one square unit is 100 m², so the field is 750 m².

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Minor Mᵢⱼ**: determinant left after deleting row i and column j.
- **Cofactor Aᵢⱼ** = (−1)^(i+j) Mᵢⱼ.
- **adj A** = transpose of the cofactor matrix.
- **A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I**, so if |A| ≠ 0, **A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|**.
- A is **singular** if |A| = 0, non-singular otherwise. Invertible ⇔ non-singular.

steps.title: Useful results (n × n)
steps.body:
- |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹
- |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|
- adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A)
- For 2 × 2 [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].

- Writing |adj A| = |A|ⁿ instead of |A|ⁿ⁻¹.

- If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O: the system may have infinitely many solutions or none — check further.

lessons.title: Continuity at a point and on an interval

scenes.text: Teacher: 'If you can draw the graph without lifting your pencil, the function is continuous there.'
Meera asks how to *prove* it without a drawing. The answer: compare the left limit, right limit and the value.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
f is **continuous at x = c** if f(c) is defined and

lim(x→c⁻) f(x) = lim(x→c⁺) f(x) = f(c).

f is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it (one-sided at closed ends).

steps.title: Continuous families
steps.body: Polynomials, sin x, cos x, eˣ, |x| are continuous everywhere; rational functions, tan x, log x are continuous wherever they are defined. Sums, differences, products, quotients (denominator ≠ 0) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

steps.title: Differentiability
steps.body:
f is differentiable at c if the left-hand derivative lim(h→0⁻)[f(c + h) − f(c)]/h equals the right-hand derivative lim(h→0⁺)[f(c + h) − f(c)]/h.

**Differentiable ⇒ continuous**, but continuous ⇏ differentiable (|x| at 0: LHD = −1, RHD = +1).

steps.title: Chain rule
steps.body: If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x))·g′(x). In Leibniz form, with u = g(x): dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

scenes.text: A startup's monthly profit first rises, then falls. The owner wants the exact months where the trend switches.
The sign of the derivative answers it: f′ > 0 means rising, f′ < 0 means falling.

steps.title: Test
steps.body:
On an interval where f is differentiable:

- f′(x) > 0 ⇒ f strictly increasing
- f′(x) < 0 ⇒ f strictly decreasing
- f′(x) = 0 throughout ⇒ f constant

Method: find f′, solve f′(x) = 0 to get critical points, split the number line, test the sign in each interval.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7
steps.body:
f′(x) = 6x² − 6x − 36 = 6(x − 3)(x + 2). Zeros: x = −2, 3.

- x < −2: f′ > 0 → increasing
- −2 < x < 3: f′ < 0 → decreasing
- x > 3: f′ > 0 → increasing

So f increases on (−∞, −2) ∪ (3, ∞) and decreases on (−2, 3).

steps.body: f′(x) = eˣ > 0 for every real x ⇒ strictly increasing.

steps.body: f′(x) = cos x − sin x. It is positive on [0, π/4) and negative on (π/4, π/2]. Increasing on [0, π/4], decreasing on [π/4, π/2].

- Forgetting to factor f′ fully.

lessons.title: Maxima and minima: first and second derivative tests

scenes.text: A hiker's altitude along a trail is a function of distance. At the top, the slope is zero; just before it is positive and just after negative.
That sign change is the first derivative test. The curvature (second derivative) is a quicker check.

steps.title: First derivative test
steps.body:
At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0 or undefined):

- f′ changes + to − ⇒ **local maximum**
- f′ changes − to + ⇒ **local minimum**
- no sign change ⇒ neither (point of inflection, e.g. x³ at 0)

steps.title: Second derivative test
steps.body:
If f′(c) = 0:

- f″(c) < 0 ⇒ local max
- f″(c) > 0 ⇒ local min
- f″(c) = 0 ⇒ test fails; use the first derivative test.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x⁴
steps.body: f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0 (test fails). f′ = 4x³ changes − to + at 0 ⇒ local min 0.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x + 1/x, x > 0
steps.body: f′ = 1 − 1/x² = 0 ⇒ x = 1. f″ = 2/x³ > 0 ⇒ local min value 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying f′(c) = 0 guarantees a max or min (x³ is a counter-example).
- Concluding 'no extremum' when f″(c) = 0 — just switch tests.
- Reporting the x-value when the question asks for the maximum **value**.

steps.title: Absolute extrema on [a, b]
steps.body: A continuous f on a closed interval attains an absolute max and min. Find them by evaluating f at **all critical points inside (a, b) and at the end-points a and b**; the largest is the absolute max, the smallest the absolute min.

steps.title: Solved: f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 2]
steps.body:
f′ = 3x² − 3 = 0 ⇒ x = 1 (x = −1 is outside).

f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(2) = 2.

Absolute max **2** at x = 2, absolute min **−2** at x = 1.

steps.title: Solved: the open box
steps.body:
Cut x cm squares: V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.

V′ = (18 − 2x)² − 4x(18 − 2x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x) = 0 ⇒ x = 3 (x = 9 gives no box).

V″ at 3 is negative (check sign change: V′ > 0 for x < 3, < 0 for 3 < x < 9) ⇒ max. V = 3·12² = **432 cm³**.

steps.title: Solved: maximum area of a rectangle with perimeter 40
steps.body: 2(x + y) = 40 ⇒ y = 20 − x. A = x(20 − x), A′ = 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10, A″ = −2 < 0 ⇒ max. The rectangle is a **10 × 10 square**, area 100.

steps.title: Optimisation recipe
steps.body: 1. Draw and name variables. 2. Write the quantity to optimise. 3. Use the constraint to reduce to one variable. 4. Differentiate, find critical points in the allowed range. 5. Confirm max/min. 6. Answer the question in words with units.
